rows.context: Studies historical conceptions of childhood through images and texts. His argument about recognizing childhood must be distinguished from a claim that parents lacked affection; Pollock challenges historical generalizations and evidence.
rows.works: L’Enfant et la vie familiale sous l’Ancien Régime (1960); Centuries of Childhood (English 1962)

strands.title: Family change, social differences and source selection

existing_sources_reused.title: Philippe Ariès, L’Enfant et la vie familiale sous l’Ancien Régime (1960); Centuries of Childhood, translated by Robert Baldick (1962).
existing_sources_reused.citation: Philippe Ariès, L’Enfant et la vie familiale sous l’Ancien Régime (1960); Centuries of Childhood, translated by Robert Baldick (1962).

verification.note: Publisher description read for historical conceptions of childhood and sources including paintings, diaries, games and school curricula; author note confirms English translation 1962, distinct from listed 1965 paperback. Original French date retained from existing record. Pollock’s primary thesis p. 31 explicitly distinguishes Ariès’s concept argument from parental affection. No full-book reading or blanket endorsement of chronology.

existing_sources_reused.title: Linda A. Pollock, Forgotten Children: Parent-Child Relations from 1500 to 1900 (Cambridge University Press, 1983).
existing_sources_reused.citation: Linda A. Pollock, Forgotten Children: Parent-Child Relations from 1500 to 1900 (Cambridge University Press, 1983).

verification.note: Publisher excerpt printed 1–10 read via OCR at https://beckassets.blob.core.windows.net/product/readingsample/401759/9780521271332_excerpt_001.pdf ; pages 2 and 10 visually collated. Page 2 separates Ariès’s childhood concept from ill-treatment and later writers’ claims about parental formality. Pages 6–9 question generalization from public policy, a royal child and secondary accounts; page 10 records Stone’s fluctuating discipline alongside his claim of increasing concern. Excerpt ends during the literature review; Pollock’s own diary-analysis chapters and endnotes unread. Prior metadata retained in history. The separately checked 1981 thesis is not treated as identical to the 1983 book; Stone’s independently read 1979 abridgment has its own source record.

verification_history.note: Indexed publisher contents checked for evidence issues: representativeness, lower-class coverage, diarists/editors, generalization and attitudes versus behavior. Original 1983 metadata confirmed in Cambridge’s Psychological Medicine review record https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/psychological-medicine/article/abs/forgotten-children-parentchild-relations-from-1500-to-1900-by-l-a-pollock-pp-334-2500-hb-950-pb-cambridge-university-press-cambridge-1983/0CF99FA3ADFDC012B93C72D92FB98A1F . Book frontmatter download stalled; no full-book reading. The separately recorded 1981 thesis provides primary argument support.

verification.note: Printed pp. 150–151 read in Persée extraction, including the sequence of publications, institutional questions, and the meeting with sociological work. P. 152 not read. The substantive interpretation is attributed to Chamboredon; books not thereby read. His 8 February 1984 death date differs from the Humathèque authority’s 9 February, so the life record adopts year precision.

reading_limit: Ariès’s complete books are unread here. Existing Pollock primary-excerpt qualifications are retained and Chamboredon is named as the substantive reader. No absence-of-parental-affection claim. French originals and Baldick’s translation remain distinct. The death-day discrepancy is kept in life research rather than resolved by assumption.

relations.relationship: Makes the historical concept of childhood a problem for family history, while prompting disputes over sources and generalization.
relations.evidence_note: The formulation retains Pollock’s distinction between concept and affection and her source criticism (1983 excerpt pp. 1–10, especially 2 and 6–9). It neither endorses Ariès’s chronology nor reassigns later writers’ stronger claims to him.

relations.relationship: Historicizes familiar family institutions and social attitudes, opening comparative questions between modernity and earlier arrangements.
relations.evidence_note: Attributed to Jean-Claude Chamboredon, 1985 pp. 150–151, on the work’s sociological questions and the family/death studies. This is a named reader’s substantive assessment, not a claim that Ariès belonged to a single sociological school.
